newsitem.title: USA: Corn prices rise on heat fears, oil also firm.
newsitem.headline: Corn prices rise on heat fears, oil also firm.

text.p: Forecasts for hot weather and little rain in the Midwest drove corn prices higher on Tuesday on concerns that the dryness will stunt growth this month.

In other markets, crude oil prices rose after a halt in Colombian shipments due to guerrilla attacks there, and gasoline prices rose sharply on expectations that a report would show a fall in stockpiles after the July 4 holiday.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for post-harvest delivery in December closed 7-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $2.56-1/2. Wheat for September delivery rose 2-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $3.38-1/4.
Meteorologists said on Tuesday a heat wave was expected in the Midwest through Friday, just as the corn crop enters the crucial pollination stage.
"The market is concerned about some heat and there will be some stress. But heat of that magnitude next week could bring more serious problems," said Dean Witter analyst Jerry Gidel.
As of Sunday, seven percent of the U.S. corn crop was silking, the early phase of the pollination or reproductive stage that determines kernel formation in the ears of corn.
Showers moved across across Iowa, Illinois and Indiana on Monday afternoon but meteorologists said the heaviest rainfall missed dry pockets in central Illinois and eastern Iowa.

Concerns about hot weather also boosted prices of post-harvest delivery prices of soybeans, with November soybeans closing up 4 cents a bushel at $6.25-3/4. July soybeans closed 8 cents a bushel lower at $8.11.
"There was support to new-crop beans on weather, and old-crop was quiet because of a lack of exports," said Gidel.
At the New York Mercantile Exchnage, oil prices rose on supply worries.

Crude oil for August delivery ended 68 cents higher at $19.67 a barrel after Occidental Petroleum halted shipments from its Cano Limon field in Colombia. The move followed attacks in the last two weeks by anti-government guerrillas.
Colombia's state oil company Ecopetrol had already halted on crude loadings on June 6 that affected at least one million barrels in exports.

"We have enough crude in the Gulf (of Mexico), but because these exports are short-haul crude, its impact is short-term and somewhat psychological," said William Brown, a trader with W.H. Brown & Co, a trading firm in New York.
Gasoline prices jumped on expectations that weekly oil industry data due on Tuesday evening from the American Petroleum Institute would show a drop in gasoline stockpiles.
August gasoline ended 1.59 cents a gallon higher at 59.94 cents.

Dealers said the inventory data should show that U.S. gasoline stocks fell between 1 million and 3 million barrels in the week ended on July 11, a period that includes the Fourth of July weekend, a popular holiday for driving.
"People are expecting draws in gasoline since demand has been strong while production has been starting to come down," said Tom Bentz, energy analyst with High Yield Analytics in New York.
August heating oil closed 1.28 cents a gallon higher at 52.95 cents.
